title: PLACEHOLDER · The confident wrong answer
scenario:
PLACEHOLDER CASE for local testing (SIG-19). Real content comes in a later ticket.

Your HR team tests an AI assistant that answers staff questions from the company policy documents. In one test it states a leave rule that is not in any document, and it sounds sure.

Source: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations

questions.prompt: What is this kind of answer called?

options.text: A hallucination: text that is wrong or not supported by the given context.
options.explanation: Right. The docs define hallucination as text that is factually incorrect or inconsistent with the given context.
A rate limit stops requests. Here the model answered, but the answer was not supported.
Caching reuses a prompt prefix. It does not make up rules.

options.text: A sign the policy documents are too short.
options.explanation: The model made up a rule that the documents don't contain. That is a hallucination, whatever the length.

questions.prompt: Which first step is simplest and lowers this risk?

options.text: Tell the assistant to always sound confident.
options.explanation: That pushes it to state guesses as facts. It makes the problem worse.

options.text: Remove the documents so the prompt is shorter.
options.explanation: Without the documents the assistant has nothing to ground its answers in.
Length does not make an answer true.

options.text: Allow it to say "I don't know" when the documents don't answer the question.
options.explanation: Right. The docs list giving the model permission to admit uncertainty as a basic strategy.

questions.prompt: You add these techniques. Can you now skip human review on high-stakes answers?

options.explanation: The docs say the techniques reduce hallucinations but do not remove them.

options.text: No. They reduce hallucinations but don't remove them, so check critical answers.
options.explanation: Right. The docs: always validate critical information, especially for high-stakes decisions.

options.text: Yes, if the answer includes a citation.
options.explanation: Citations make answers easier to check. Someone still has to check the high-stakes ones.

options.text: Yes, if the model is a newer one.
options.explanation: The docs say even the most advanced models can hallucinate.
